content: An ovarian cyst is a fluid-filled sac that develops on or within an ovary. Functional ovarian cysts are a specific type of cyst that forms during the menstrual cycle and are not related to cancer or other diseases. Symptoms of Ovarian Cysts: Ovarian cysts often do not cause symptoms. However, when symptoms occur, they typically include pain or a delayed menstrual period. Pain is more likely if the cyst: Becomes large Bleeds Ruptures Is bumped during sexual intercourse Twists or causes torsion of the Fallopian tube Symptoms of ovarian cysts may include: Abdominal bloating or swelling Pain during bowel movements Pelvic pain shortly before or after the start of a menstrual period Pain during intercourse or pelvic pain with movement Persistent, dull pelvic pain Sudden, severe pelvic pain accompanied by nausea and vomiting, which may indicate ovarian torsion or cyst rupture with internal bleeding Changes in menstrual periods are uncommon with follicular cysts but more frequent with corpus luteum cysts. Spotting or abnormal bleeding may occur with some cysts. Causes of Ovarian Cysts: During each menstrual cycle, a follicle grows on the ovary to develop an egg. If the egg is not released, the follicle may form a follicular cyst. A corpus luteum cyst can form after the egg is released, often containing a small amount of blood. Ovarian cysts are relatively common, especially during a woman’s reproductive years (from puberty to menopause). They are less common after menopause. No specific risk factors have been identified. Functional ovarian cysts are distinct from ovarian tumors (including ovarian cancer) or hormone-related conditions like polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Fertility drugs can lead to ovarian hyperstimulation, a condition where multiple large cysts form on the ovaries. These typically resolve after a menstrual period or pregnancy. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: Contact a healthcare provider if you experience symptoms of an ovarian cyst, severe pain, or abnormal bleeding. Seek medical attention if you have persistent symptoms for at least two weeks, such as: Feeling full quickly when eating Loss of appetite Unintentional weight loss Diagnosis: Ovarian cysts may be discovered during a physical exam or an ultrasound performed for another reason. Ultrasound is commonly used to diagnose ovarian cysts. Follow-up imaging may be recommended in 4–6 weeks to ensure the cyst has resolved. Additional imaging tests, if needed, may include: CT scan Doppler flow studies MRI During a pelvic exam, a healthcare provider may feel the cyst. Blood tests may be ordered, such as: CA-125 test to evaluate for possible cancer in postmenopausal women or those with abnormal ultrasound findings Hormone level tests (e.g., LH, FSH, estradiol, testosterone) Serum HCG (pregnancy test) Treatment Options: Functional ovarian cysts typically do not require treatment and often resolve within 8–12 weeks. Birth control pills may be prescribed for 4–6 weeks to prevent the formation of new cysts. Long-term use can reduce the likelihood of new cyst development but does not shrink existing cysts, which often resolve on their own. Surgery may be necessary to remove the cyst or ovary to rule out cancer, especially in cases of: Complex ovarian cysts that do not resolve Symptomatic cysts that persist Simple ovarian cysts larger than 5–10 centimeters Postmenopausal or perimenopausal women Types of surgery include: Exploratory laparotomy Pelvic laparoscopy to remove the cyst or ovary If a condition like PCOS is causing the cysts, other treatments may be recommended. Prognosis: Cysts in premenopausal women are more likely to resolve on their own. Postmenopausal women have a higher risk of ovarian cancer. Possible Complications: Complications depend on the underlying cause of the cysts and may include: Bleeding Rupture Malignant changes Torsion (twisting) Prevention: If you frequently develop functional ovarian cysts and are not trying to conceive, taking hormonal medications (e.g., birth control pills) can prevent the growth of follicles and reduce the risk of cyst formation.
